extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly (general educated public, amateur naturalists, and agriculturists), late-19th-century science-interested audience
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and prescribing the Javanese solar-year division based on star positions and noon-shadow lengths, with month-by-month observational markers and corresponding farming rules for planting and harvesting in tropical Java.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis — labyrinthine vertigo
rubrics_metrics.description: We can diagnose his life-long disease as labyrinthine vertigo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifying features cited: paroxysmal nature of the affection with long intervals of immunity; deafness beginning before twenty and persistent ear defect; fits of giddiness often triggered by slight head movements; paroxysms that cause great constitutional disturbance though sometimes brief; historical quotations showing frequent 'giddy' episodes (journal excerpts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis — dementia with aphasia
rubrics_metrics.description: His insanity is diagnosed as dementia with aphasia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting evidence: 'emotional depression amounting to melancholia,' 'much water in the brain' (probably sub-arachnoid effusion) as evidence of dementia; presence of aphasia characterized by scraps of reasonable language coming automatically while intentional speech effort fails; plaster-cast evidence of right-sided hemiplegia suggesting localized brain disease producing paralysis and aphasia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Osteological/cast evidence for neurological signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaster-cast and skull observations as diagnostic evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes: cast of interior of skull shows 'enormous development of the vessels within the cranium, the very small anterior lobes, the great size of the glandulae Pacchionian, the exceedingly small cerebellum... the immense size of the posterior and middle lobes' and a deep indentation showing where calvarium had been sawn; plaster-cast shows right-sided hemiplegia; such osteological features corroborate clinical diagnosis but must be weighed with caution (busts show variable head-forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal inference cautions in historical diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish direct extension of local disease to brain from indirect effects (e.g., chronic vertigo causing depression vs. brain disease causing mental disorder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author emphasizes uncertainty whether vertigo directly extended to brain to cause insanity, vs indirect effect via profound depression; notes absence of authenticated early outbreak accounts and warns against over-reading single sources (e.g., Wilde's account).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concept — bulb growth as 'unfolding' (hyacinth bulbs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A bulb does not grow as an ordinary plant grows, solely by means of carbon from the air under sunlight; its growth should be called its 'unfolding' because it contains within itself everything necessary for development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implications for cultivation/experiment: bulbs will sprout in darkness or diffused light from stored reserves; leaves will be blanched without light but flowers will retain color; bulbs represent several years' accumulation and can be forced by preventing flowering to produce finer trusses later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanism — seed/bulb germination uses internal energetic materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Germination involves slow combustion: oxygen combines with starches and albumens stored in seed or bulb to give heat and motion that drive early growth until photosynthesis resumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains analogy to engine/combustion; after reserves are used, plant must unfold leaves to sunlight to begin assimilation of fresh carbon and hydrogen. Observable consequences include measurable heat during germination (malting) and motion (growth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of light on leaves vs flowers (hyacinth observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bulb is grown entirely in the dark, leaves will be blanched and almost colorless, while the flowers will be just as brilliantly colored as in light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasoning given: green pigment (chlorophyll) requires light to form and is the 'active agent of digestion' in leaves, whereas flower pigment is 'always due to oxidation alone' and is little dependent on sunlight; even bulbs grown away from window will have paler leaves but normally colored flowers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ecological/evolutionary rationale for storage organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants in certain families (lilies, narcissus, crocus, orchids, tubers, roots) store reserves in bulbs, corms, tubers or thickened roots to survive seasonal dieback and to give advantage to offspring or perennial growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These storage habits are adaptive: they allow early flowering and growth season-to-season and reduce risk of predation by keeping reserves underground; humans have further selected for such traits in domesticated crops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Javanese calendar method — dividing the solar year by shadow length
rubrics_metrics.description: The Javanese adjust the division of their solar year by measuring the length and direction of the noon shadow (on 21 June vs 21 December) and dividing these lengths into unequal parts to create six unequal time intervals which then determine twelve unequal months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method details: length of shadow on June 21 divided into four equal parts, on Dec 21 divided into two equal parts, yielding six measures corresponding to unequal time intervals; first day of year corresponds to June 21 of Gregorian reckoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: First month (Kasci) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: First month (Kasci), forty-one days, from the 21st of June to the 31st of July inclusive. Orion and the Pleiades are visible in the east, respectively 25° and 45° above the horizon. The sun turns back toward the south; a man's shadow at noon reaches four feet south. The fresh-water fish hoak bettik has one spot on its head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farmers' rule: 'It is time to plant the second crop of rice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Second month (Kara) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Second month (Kara), twenty-three days long, from the 1st to the 23d of August. The Pleiades are in the zenith, Orion 70° above the eastern horizon. The hoak bettik has two spots. The sun goes farther toward the south. A man's shadow at noon measures two feet south.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit farmers' timing cues tied to star positions and shadow length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third month (Tetiga) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Third month (Tetiga), twenty-four days, from the 24th of August to the 16th of September. Before sunrise the Pleiades are 70° above the western horizon, Orion in the zenith. The leaves begin to fall from the trees. The hoak bettik has three spots. The noonday shadow measures one foot south.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farmers' rule: 'The second crop of rice begins to ripen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourth month (Ifapat) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth month (Ifapat), twenty-five days, from the 17th of September to the 11th of October. Before sunrise the Pleiades are 50° and Orion 70° above the western horizon. The glatik s (rice-birds) fall upon the fields in multitudes; fruit-trees have new buds and fresh leaves; randoe fruits are ripe; cotton appears and begins to fall. The sun rises in the east and casts no shadow at noon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farmers' rule: 'Harvest begins.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fifth month (ICelima) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Fifth month (ICelima), twenty-seven days, from the 12th of October till the 7th of November. Medical plants called lempoeygang begin to put out new roots; swallows inaog terrik collect on mountain slopes; tjekithoets sing more; the iwak bettik has five spots. A man's shadow measures a foot north.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farmers' rule: 'Plant maize.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Sixth month (Tumern) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Sixth month (Tumern), forty-three days, from the 8th of November till the 20th of December. Heavy rains begin. Plant rice. Orion visible in eastern horizon immediately after sunset. Woodcocks appear and resort to ponds; beetles (koioangaus) come down from mountains to lay eggs on half-submerged herbage; spiders (kemlandmgaus) change web orientation. The iwak bettih has six spots. The sun advances toward the south, and a man's shadow measures two feet north.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit farmers' rule: 'Plant rice.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Seventh month (Tepitoe) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Seventh month (Tepitoe), forty-three days, from the 21st of December till the 2d of February. Orion and the Pleiades are respectively 25° and 45° above the eastern horizon. Rice-planting is continued. The distillable herb wood-ivy (ouvi) is ripe. Beetle eggs open. The iwak bettih has seven spots. The sun turns back toward the north, and the shadow measures nearly three feet north.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continued rice-planting is the recommended agricultural activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eighth month (Iterraloe) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Eighth month (Iterraloe), twenty-six days, from the 3d to the 28th of February. Orion is in the zenith, the Pleiades are 70° above the west. Rice-planting is completed. The iwak bettik has eight spots. The glagahs begin to bloom. The sun rises in the east.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates the completion of rice-planting and onset of blooming of certain plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ninth month (Kesauga) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Ninth month (Kesauga), twenty-five days, from the 1st till the 25th of March. Orion is in the zenith at six o'clock in the evening, the Pleiades 70° up in the west. The iwak bettik has nine spots. The flowers of the glagah fall. The sun crosses the equator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signifies flowering end and equinoctial crossing for seasonal decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenth month (Sepoeloch) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Tenth month (Sepoeloch), twenty-four days, from the 25th of March till the 17th of April. The Pleiades are 45°, Orion 65° up in the west. The spots of the iwak bettik have disappeared. The rice is ripe and the harvest begins. The sun is in the north, and the shadow measures from one to two feet south.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farmers' rule: 'The rice is ripe and the harvest begins.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Eleventh month (Destha) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Eleventh month (Destha), twenty-three days, from the 18th of April till the 10th of May. The rice-harvest everywhere. The nights are cold and the days are the shortest in the year. Orion is visible 16° up in the west at half past six in the evening. The Pleiades are invisible. The randoe-trocs begin to bloom. The sun comes toward the north and the shadow measures three feet south.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates harvest conclusion and short-day conditions important for cropping decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelfth month (Sada) — observational markers and agricultural rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Twelfth month (Sada), forty-one days, from the 11th of May till the 20th of June. The Pleiades may be seen at half past five in the morning, a little later Orion. The rice-harvest is finished, cotton and indigo are planted, and the ground is prepared for maize. The shadow measures three feet south, and the sun goes to its northernmost point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farmers' rule: final harvest activities finished; plant cotton and indigo and prepare ground for maize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental method to test spontaneous generation (Pasteur)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pasteur's test: boil a suitable organic infusion in glass flasks, hermetically seal them while boiling to exclude air-born germs, then take flasks to different localities and later break the necks to admit air; observe whether different localities produce different organisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logical expectation: if organisms arise spontaneously from the atmosphere alone, the products would be the same where bottles are broken; if life depends on introduction of extraneous organisms/germs from the air, differing atmospheric contents in different places will produce different results. Pasteur's experiments showed differences consistent with germ introduction, supporting his panspermy theory and arguing against spontaneous generation.
